name: What to Do When Fresh Bathroom Paint Peels in Los Angeles Homes

mainEntity.name: What should I do if interior paint starts peeling or bubbling in a Los Angeles bathroom within a year of being repainted?
mainEntity.text: What should I do if interior paint starts peeling or bubbling in a Los Angeles bathroom within a year of being repainted?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your recently repainted Los Angeles bathroom starts peeling, bubbling, or flaking within a year, treat it as both a moisture and workmanship issue. First, check for obvious water sources: active leaks, failed caulking around tubs or showers, or chronic condensation on walls and ceilings. Ensure the exhaust fan is working and used long enough after showers to clear steam. Document the problem with photos and review your painter’s warranty; most reputable contractors expect interior paint to last longer than a year in normal conditions and may treat this as a callback, especially if they specified the products. Proper repair involves scraping and sanding all loose or bubbled paint edges, not just spot-touching. Glossy or previously peeling areas should be primed with a moisture- and mildew-resistant bonding primer before repainting. The topcoat should be a high-quality bathroom-rated or mildew-resistant paint in at least an eggshell or satin sheen, which sheds moisture better than flat. Ask your painter what they believe caused the failure—poor adhesion to old glossy paint, skipping primer, or ongoing moisture—and what changes they will make in their process. Address both the paint and the underlying moisture issue; otherwise, the problem is likely to return.
acceptedAnswer.description: Peeling or bubbling interior paint in a Los Angeles bathroom within a year usually indicates moisture or prep problems. Increase ventilation, check for leaks, and contact the painter about warranty coverage. Proper repair typically requires scraping loose areas, priming with a moisture-resistant primer, and repainting with a suitable bathroom paint.
